ends.label: Equality with employment
ends.statement: Combine fair wages and full employment with price stability and growth.

ends.label: Wage-earner influence
ends.statement: Distribute wealth more evenly and strengthen wage-earner influence through co-ownership while supporting pensions and capital formation.

means.label: Solidaristic bargaining and adjustment
means.description: Peak labor and employer organizations set central wage frames while public labor-market institutions support training, matching, and mobility.

means.label: Capped wage-earner fund boards
means.description: Five government-appointed pension-system boards invested payroll- and profit-tax receipts under funding, ownership, and voting limits.

cases.name: Swedish Rehn–Meidner policy complex
cases.boundary: Begins with the 1951 LO program, focuses on the 1956–1982 centralized-bargaining window, and ends with the 1983 breakdown. It excludes the later enacted wage-earner funds.
cases.relationship: Influenced by Swedish organized labor and social-democratic policymaking; not an embodiment of the whole tradition.
conditions: Macroeconomic and labor-market policies operating alongside wage bargaining

statements.text: Wage inequality was stable before the late 1960s and declined rapidly thereafter; deliberate union policy likely explains a substantial share of the 1970s compression.
statements.limitation: The study disputes a simple account of 1960s compression and does not identify one cause for every wage change.

statements.text: Reduced interindustry wage differentials were associated with higher aggregate output and productivity, while within-industry compression was not.
statements.limitation: The association does not establish transferability or isolate every concurrent institution.

rivalExplanations: Economic structure, macroeconomic policy, wage drift, and external shocks may explain outcomes attributed to solidaristic wage policy.
Molinder finds that wage compression coincided with falling growth and structural change, qualifying a simple restructuring-success account.

cases.name: Enacted Swedish wage-earner funds
cases.boundary: Covers the five enacted pension-system fund boards through abolition and keeps them distinct from the more open-ended 1975 Meidner proposal.
cases.relationship: A contested compromise within Swedish social-democratic politics, not a definition of the tradition.
conditions: Polarized conflict between organized labor and business
Government appointment and parliamentary control of the rules

statements.text: The arrangement created five independent government-appointed boards with worker-interest representation, specified tax funding, and company voting limits.
statements.limitation: Formal statutory rules do not establish how authority operated in practice.

statements.text: At the end of 1991 the funds held approximately 2.6 percent of stock-exchange value and generally operated as investment companies rather than controlling owners.
statements.limitation: Aggregate ownership does not capture every firm-level influence or unlisted investment.

statements.text: The five boards were abolished at the end of 1991 and their assets transferred to a liquidation board.
statements.limitation: The abolition date alone does not establish the relative importance of ideology, electoral change, performance, or economic conditions.

rivalExplanations: Limited control can be interpreted as dilution of an ownership-transfer mechanism.
The same limits can be interpreted as safeguards against concentrated delegated power.

trace.expectedInteraction: Wage compression should shift gains toward lower-paid workers, while collective capital claims should alter who receives profit and exercises ownership rights.
trace.assessment: The arrangements affected wage distribution, but the evidence presented here does not establish a comparable reduction in private wealth concentration.
